doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

title: The Original Dixieland Jass Band and James Reese Europe
summary: They discuss the first jazz recording and an argument with a man who claimed James Reese Europe.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Frank Foster said the coolest, succinct — he said, jazz is the experience — came out of the experience of a black musician in America and no one’s ever going to tell me different. But now our culture is so — he had a really good way of saying it. I think there’s some things that we wish happened differently. For instance, tomorrow is the hundredth anniversary of the Original Dixieland Jass Band.
It would have been nice if King Oliver —
Could have had that historical distinction.

Yeah. It would have been nice. And this controversy too, I’ve heard people say, “Wasn’t James Reese Europe the first person to put jazz on record?” I had a guy pigeonhole me. We were on some panel together and he got me in a corner and he was pushing hard. And he said, “Come on you have to agree with me that James Reese Europe was the first —” I just said, “Listen man, I know what you’re trying to do. I know you don’t like the fact that the ODJB, a white group, was the first.” This happened to be a black Muslim by the way. And so he was pushing that whole black thing. And I was like, “I’m sorry man, I just can’t go with it.” I mean what Europe was playing was peppy and syncopated, but it wasn’t jazz in any shape or form. It wasn’t jazz. And you can’t say that, it’s just not true. And even though it was 1914, you can’t say it was the first jazz. So he didn’t go with it. He still thought I was wrong. But you’re right. I might agree with you. I wish it had been a little different. Because really, when you hear the ODJB records, I don’t want to say they’re corny but —
They’re corny. Well you’ve got to think of the time it was but we know now it wasn’t the real thing that could have been captured.
It’s close. Close enough for jazz.
